new_entities.name: Social media restriction intervention
new_entities.description: An intervention that deliberately restricts or reduces social media use to improve mental health or wellbeing.

edges.effect_quant: A 2025 meta-analysis of 20 randomized controlled trials and 56 effect sizes found a small positive overall effect of social media detox on wellbeing, but two individual randomized trials in 67 and 122 participants reported largely neutral short-term wellbeing effects.
edges.population: adolescents, students, or young adults assigned to intentionally reduce or cap social media use
edges.mechanism: Reducing social media may lower social comparison, fear of missing out, and compulsive checking, but benefits likely depend on whether use was excessive or distress-driven at baseline.
edges.summary: Restriction interventions show a small pooled wellbeing benefit overall, but individual randomized trials are mixed and often neutral over short follow-up windows. The most defensible classification is mildly protective overall, with benefit likely depending on baseline overuse, distress, and intervention intensity.
edges.caveats: Do not present social media restriction as a universally effective mental-health treatment. Some trials show null results, and short intervention windows may underestimate or miss subgroup-specific benefits.

evidence.citation: Maerevoet M et al 2025 Front Public Health
evidence.notes: Causal effects of social media use on self-esteem, mindfulness, sleep and emotional well-being: a social media restriction study.

evidence.notes: Effects of restricting social media usage on wellbeing and performance: A randomized control trial among students.
